claim: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) is caused by CCTG repeat expansions in the CNBP gene.
source: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2; MIM#602668) is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness, myotonia, myalgia, calf hypertrophy, and multiorgan involvement with cataract, cardiac conduction defects, and endocrine disorders (Meola and Cardani, 2015; Montagnese et al., 2017). The disease is caused by a (CCTG)n repeat expansion in intron 1 of the CNBP gene (previously ZNF9; MIM*116955) on chromosome 3q21.3 (Liquori et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Liquori et al., 2001) and established scientific knowledge about DM2.

claim: DM2 CCTG repeat expansions comprise 75 to >11,000 units.
source: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) is caused by CCTG repeat expansions in the CNBP gene, comprising 75 to >11,000 units and featuring extensive mosaicism, making it challenging to sequence fully expanded alleles.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by established knowledge about DM2 repeat expansion sizes.

claim: DM2 expansions feature extensive mosaicism.
source: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) is caused by CCTG repeat expansions in the CNBP gene, comprising 75 to >11,000 units and featuring extensive mosaicism, making it challenging to sequence fully expanded alleles.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript showing variability in repeat lengths within individuals.

claim: The study used PCR-free Cas9-mediated nanopore sequencing to characterize CNBP repeat expansions in nine DM2 patients.
source: To overcome these limitations, we used PCR-free Cas9-mediated nanopore sequencing to characterize CNBP repeat expansions at the single-nucleotide level in nine DM2 patients.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental approach used in the study, which is detailed in the methods and results sections.

claim: The study sequenced an entire ~50 kbp expansion, which has not been achieved previously for DM2 or any other repeat-expansion disorders.
source: We also sequenced an entire ~50 kbp expansion, which has not been achieved previously for DM2 or any other repeat-expansion disorders.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing sequencing of a 46.6 kbp expansion and comparison with previous literature on repeat expansion sequencing.

claim: Only two DM2 samples featured the expected pure CCTG repeat pattern in the expanded alleles.
source: Interestingly, in the expanded alleles, only two DM2 samples featured the expected pure CCTG repeat pattern, while the other seven presented also TCTG blocks at the 3′ end, which have not been reported before in DM2 patients, but confirmed hereby with orthogonal methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data analysis and confirmed by QP-PCR validation.

claim: Seven DM2 samples presented TCTG blocks at the 3′ end of the expansion, which have not been reported before in DM2 patients.
source: Interestingly, in the expanded alleles, only two DM2 samples featured the expected pure CCTG repeat pattern, while the other seven presented also TCTG blocks at the 3′ end, which have not been reported before in DM2 patients, but confirmed hereby with orthogonal methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data and validated by orthogonal QP-PCR methods.

claim: DM2 is characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness, myotonia, myalgia, calf hypertrophy, and multiorgan involvement with cataract, cardiac conduction defects, and endocrine disorders.
source: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2; MIM#602668) is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness, myotonia, myalgia, calf hypertrophy, and multiorgan involvement with cataract, cardiac conduction defects, and endocrine disorders (Meola and Cardani, 2015; Montagnese et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing DM2 clinical features.

claim: The CNBP gene is located on chromosome 3q21.3.
source: The disease is caused by a (CCTG)n repeat expansion in intron 1 of the CNBP gene (previously ZNF9; MIM*116955) on chromosome 3q21.3 (Liquori et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the gene discovery study and established genomic knowledge.

claim: The CCTG repeat tract is part of a complex (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x motif in healthy-range alleles.
source: The CCTG repeat tract is part of a complex (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x motif that, in healthy-range alleles, is generally interrupted by one or more GCTG, TCTG, or ACTG (NCTG) motifs that confer repeat stability (Radvanszky et al., 2013; Mahyera et al., 2018; Guo and Lam, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on CNBP repeat structure.

claim: In healthy-range alleles, the CCTG repeat is generally interrupted by one or more GCTG, TCTG, or ACTG (NCTG) motifs that confer repeat stability.
source: The CCTG repeat tract is part of a complex (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x motif that, in healthy-range alleles, is generally interrupted by one or more GCTG, TCTG, or ACTG (NCTG) motifs that confer repeat stability (Radvanszky et al., 2013; Mahyera et al., 2018; Guo and Lam, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on repeat stability mechanisms.

claim: Nonpathogenic alleles contain up to 26 CCTG repeat units.
source: Nonpathogenic alleles contain up to 26 CCTG repeat units, whereas premutations are composed of <75 'pure' CCTG blocks whose clinical significance remains unclear (Mahyera et al., 2018; Botta et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on CNBP repeat thresholds.

claim: In DM2 patients, the number of repeats is between ~75 and >11,000 units.
source: In DM2 patients, the number of repeats is between ~75 and >11,000 units, among the largest reported so far in repeat-expansion disorders (Depienne and Mandel, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and established knowledge about DM2 repeat sizes.

claim: DM2 expansions are among the largest reported so far in repeat-expansion disorders.
source: In DM2 patients, the number of repeats is between ~75 and >11,000 units, among the largest reported so far in repeat-expansion disorders (Depienne and Mandel, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature comparing repeat expansion sizes across disorders.

claim: The DM2 mutation shows marked somatic instability and tends to increase in length over time within the same individual.
source: The DM2 mutation shows marked somatic instability and tends to increase in length over time within the same individual, but it does not show a strong bias toward intergenerational expansion, and genetic anticipation is rarely seen in DM2 families (Liquori et al., 2001; Kamsteeg et al., 2012; Mahyera et al., 2018; Thornton, 2014; Udd et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on DM2 mutation dynamics.

claim: The DM2 mutation does not show a strong bias toward intergenerational expansion.
source: The DM2 mutation shows marked somatic instability and tends to increase in length over time within the same individual, but it does not show a strong bias toward intergenerational expansion, and genetic anticipation is rarely seen in DM2 families (Liquori et al., 2001; Kamsteeg et al., 2012; Mahyera et al., 2018; Thornton, 2014; Udd et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on DM2 inheritance patterns.

claim: Genetic anticipation is rarely seen in DM2 families.
source: The DM2 mutation shows marked somatic instability and tends to increase in length over time within the same individual, but it does not show a strong bias toward intergenerational expansion, and genetic anticipation is rarely seen in DM2 families (Liquori et al., 2001; Kamsteeg et al., 2012; Mahyera et al., 2018; Thornton, 2014; Udd et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on DM2 clinical genetics.

claim: Genotype-phenotype studies in DM2 patients did not reveal significant associations between disease severity and the number of CCTG repeats.
source: The few genotype–phenotype studies reported so far in DM2 patients did not reveal any significant associations between the severity of the disease, including the age at onset, and the number of CCTG repeats (Day et al., 2003; Udd et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published genotype-phenotype studies.

claim: Southern blot analysis fails to detect the DM2 mutation in about 20% of known carriers.
source: Because of the extremely large size of the CCTG expansions and somatic instability of the repeat, Southern blot fails to detect the DM2 mutation in about 20% of known carriers, whose expansion length remains undeterminable.
evidence: The claim is stated in the discussion and reflects known limitations of Southern blot analysis for DM2.

claim: Current best practice for DM2 genetic testing relies mainly on PCR-based approaches.
source: According to international guidelines, current best practice for DM2 genetic testing relies mainly on PCR-based approaches (Botta et al., 2006; Kamsteeg et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to international diagnostic guidelines.

claim: LR-PCR and QP-PCR achieve a ~99% detection rate for DM2 mutations.
source: When only one allele is visible, (CCTG)n expansions can be identified by long-range PCR (LR-PCR) or quadruplet-repeat primed PCR (QP-PCR), leading to a ~99% detection rate (Kamsteeg et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published diagnostic guidelines.

claim: Southern blot analysis for DM2 has a sensitivity of ~80%.
source: However, neither method can define the exact length of large DM2 expansions, which requires the Southern blot analysis of digested genomic DNA and has a sensitivity of ~80% (Day et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on diagnostic methods.

claim: Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing can generate reads >100 kbp in length.
source: The latter can generate reads >100 kbp in length (Payne et al., 2019; Iyer et al., 2022) and recently demonstrated valuable for the analysis of very long repetitive elements, like telomeric and centromeric regions in the completion of human genome (Sergey et al., 2022; Consortium and The Telomere-to-telomere T T, 2022) and microsatellite expansions in the pathogenic range (Stevanovski et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on ONT sequencing capabilities.

claim: The longest allele characterized by third-generation sequencing prior to this study was a 21-kbp allele of the C9orf72 gene.
source: The longest allele thus far characterized by third-generation sequencing is a 21-kbp allele of the C9orf72 gene that causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on repeat expansion sequencing.

claim: PacBio reads do not exceed 20 kbp in a PCR-free enrichment.
source: Importantly, PacBio reads do not exceed 20 kbp in a PCR-free enrichment (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2021; Ebbert et al., 2018; Hafford-Tear et al., 2019; Höijer et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2017; Wieben et al., 2019), and would not completely span DM2 pathogenic expansions (20 kbp on average, but up to 50 kbp).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on PacBio sequencing limitations.

claim: The study analyzed nine DM2 patients (six males and three females, mean age = 46.4 ± 20 years).
source: We analyzed nine DM2 patients (six males and three females, mean age = 46.4 ± 20 years) with existing molecular diagnoses based on a combination of PCR-based approaches (SR-PCR, LR-PCR, and QP-PCR) to detect the presence of (CCTG)n expansions in the CNBP gene (Table 1).
evidence: The claim describes the study cohort and is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Four patients were familial cases (A1–A4) whereas patients B, C, D, E, and F were sporadic cases.
source: Four patients were familial cases (A1–A4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) whereas patients B, C, D, E, and F were sporadic cases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the pedigree shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Southern blot analysis suggested that the size of the microsatellite ranged from 20 to about 40 kbp.
source: This suggested that the size of the microsatellite ranged from 20 to about 40 kbp (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Table 1.

claim: Eight short interrupted alleles had the structure (TG)17–24 (TCTG)6–9 (CCTG)5–7 GCTG CCTG TCTG (CCTG)7.
source: The characterization of normal CNBP alleles by SR-PCR and Sanger sequencing revealed the presence of eight short interrupted alleles with the structure (TG)17–24 (TCTG)6–9 (CCTG)5–7 GCTG CCTG TCTG (CCTG)7 and one short uninterrupted allele with the structure (TG)19 (TCTG)9 (CCTG)12, matching our previous results for an Italian population (Botta et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: One short uninterrupted allele had the structure (TG)19 (TCTG)9 (CCTG)12.
source: The characterization of normal CNBP alleles by SR-PCR and Sanger sequencing revealed the presence of eight short interrupted alleles with the structure (TG)17–24 (TCTG)6–9 (CCTG)5–7 GCTG CCTG TCTG (CCTG)7 and one short uninterrupted allele with the structure (TG)19 (TCTG)9 (CCTG)12, matching our previous results for an Italian population (Botta et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Cas9-mediated sequencing achieved good target coverage with 346 ± 64 reads on the CNBP locus.
source: Cas9-mediated sequencing achieved good target coverage in all experiments, with 346 ± 64 reads (mean ± standard error of the mean) on the CNBP locus (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Singleplex runs had consistently lower background than multiplex runs (0.08× vs. 0.57×).
source: Singleplex runs had consistently lower background than multiplex runs (0.08× vs. 0.57×), and thus achieved a higher average fold enrichment (3521- vs. 637-fold) (Figure 1B, C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data comparing singleplex and multiplex experiments shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Singleplex runs achieved a higher average fold enrichment than multiplex runs (3521- vs. 637-fold).
source: Singleplex runs had consistently lower background than multiplex runs (0.08× vs. 0.57×), and thus achieved a higher average fold enrichment (3521- vs. 637-fold) (Figure 1B, C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data comparing singleplex and multiplex experiments shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: For each DM2 patient, a mean total of 105,737 PASS reads were generated, 308 of which were on target.
source: Collectively, for each DM2 patient, we generated a mean total of 105,737 PASS reads, 308 of which were on target (Figure 1D) and 186 of which completely spanned the normal or expanded alleles (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing statistics shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 186 reads completely spanned the normal or expanded alleles on average per patient.
source: Collectively, for each DM2 patient, we generated a mean total of 105,737 PASS reads, 308 of which were on target (Figure 1D) and 186 of which completely spanned the normal or expanded alleles (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing statistics shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Complete sequences represented ~78% of normal repeat-spanning reads and ~22% of expanded repeat-spanning reads.
source: Only these 'complete sequences' were used for subsequent analysis, representing ~78% and~22% of the normal and expanded repeat-spanning reads, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The complex (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x (NCTG)y (CCTG)z repeat ranged in size from 122 to 141 bp in normal alleles.
source: The de novo assembly of reads derived from the normal CNBP alleles in DM2 patients (145 on average per sample, IQR = 67; Figure 1E) showed that the complex (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x (NCTG)y (CCTG)z repeat ranged in size from 122 to 141 bp, corresponding to 12–15 CCTG quadruplets (Table 2 and Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data analysis shown in Table 2 and Figure 2B.

claim: Normal alleles contained 12–15 CCTG quadruplets.
source: The de novo assembly of reads derived from the normal CNBP alleles in DM2 patients (145 on average per sample, IQR = 67; Figure 1E) showed that the complex (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x (NCTG)y (CCTG)z repeat ranged in size from 122 to 141 bp, corresponding to 12–15 CCTG quadruplets (Table 2 and Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data analysis shown in Table 2 and Figure 2B.

claim: The size and repeat pattern of normal alleles determined by ONT sequencing were largely consistent with Sanger sequencing data (99.5% mean accuracy, Pearson's r=0.971, p < 0.0001).
source: The size and repeat pattern in each patient were largely consistent with the Sanger sequencing data (99.5% mean accuracy, Pearson's r=0.971, p < 0.0001; Figure 2C), with six patients showing a perfect match, two differing at a single-nucleotide position and only one differing at two nucleotide positions (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ONT and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2C and Table 2.

claim: Reads derived from the expanded alleles ranged from 344 bp to as much as 46.6 kbp.
source: Reads derived from the expanded alleles (41 on average per sample, IQR = 11; Figure 1E) ranged from 344 bp to as much as 46.6 kbp (Figure 2D), confirming the presence of extremely large expansions in these patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The 46.6 kbp expansion is the longest repeat expansion analyzed thus far at single-nucleotide resolution.
source: To our knowledge, the latter is the longest repeat expansion analyzed thus far at single-nucleotide resolution (Mizuguchi et al., 2021; Sone et al., 2019; Giesselmann et al., 2019; Wallace et al., 2021) and is one of the longest DNA fragments captured by Cas9-mediated enrichment with no specific adjustment (Gilpatrick et al., 2020; Iyer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published literature on repeat expansion sequencing.

claim: The 46.6 kbp expansion is one of the longest DNA fragments captured by Cas9-mediated enrichment with no specific adjustment.
source: To our knowledge, the latter is the longest repeat expansion analyzed thus far at single-nucleotide resolution (Mizuguchi et al., 2021; Sone et al., 2019; Giesselmann et al., 2019; Wallace et al., 2021) and is one of the longest DNA fragments captured by Cas9-mediated enrichment with no specific adjustment (Gilpatrick et al., 2020; Iyer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published literature on Cas9-mediated enrichment.

claim: The number of repetitive quadruplets varied from 1371 to 4421 on average per sample.
source: Considering average values per sample, the number of repetitive quadruplets varied from 1371 to 4421, corresponding to expansion lengths of 5485–17,685 bp.
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data analysis.

claim: Average expansion lengths ranged from 5485–17,685 bp.
source: Considering average values per sample, the number of repetitive quadruplets varied from 1371 to 4421, corresponding to expansion lengths of 5485–17,685 bp.
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data analysis.

claim: The longest molecule sequenced with ONT largely agreed with the Southern blot estimates (Pearson's r = 0.6840, p = 0.0422).
source: Moreover, in each patient, the longest molecule sequenced with ONT (derived from the expanded allele) largely agreed with the Southern blot estimates (Pearson's r = 0.6840, p = 0.0422, Figure 2E), with the exception of sample (B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ONT and Southern blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The mean size of reads derived from the expanded allele was consistently more variable than that from the normal allele (65% ± 0.091 vs. 4% ± 0.002).
source: Even within the same individual, the mean size of reads derived from the expanded allele was consistently more variable than that from the normal allele (65% ± 0.091 vs. 4% ± 0.002; Figure 2B–D, Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data analysis shown in Figures 2B-D and Figure 3.

claim: The pronounced variability within each DM2 patient indicates extensive mosaicism.
source: Such pronounced variability within each DM2 patient indicates extensive mosaicism, in agreement with previous reports (Liquori et al., 2001; Bachinski et al., 2003; Day et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on repeat length variability and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The uninterrupted (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x motif was found at the 5′ end of the repeat locus in all nine patients.
source: The uninterrupted (TG)v (TCTG)w (CCTG)x motif that characterizes expanded CNBP alleles was found at the 5′ end of the repeat locus in all nine patients (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 3.

claim: When present, the TCTG motif was detected in 11%–86% of the expanded allele reads.
source: When present, the TCTG motif was detected in a highly variable fraction of sequences (11%–86% of the expanded allele reads, Table 3), and differed widely in length (40–8000 bp) between donors and within the same individual (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data shown in Table 3 and Figure 3.

claim: The TCTG motif differed widely in length (40–8000 bp) between donors and within the same individual.
source: When present, the TCTG motif was detected in a highly variable fraction of sequences (11%–86% of the expanded allele reads, Table 3), and differed widely in length (40–8000 bp) between donors and within the same individual (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data shown in Table 3 and Figure 3.

claim: QP-PCR analysis using primer P4TCTG revealed an electrophoretic profile compatible with the presence of (TCTG)n downstream of the (CCTG)n expansion in seven DM2 samples.
source: In agreement with the ONT data, QP-PCR analysis using primer P4TCTG revealed an electrophoretic profile compatible with the presence of (TCTG)n downstream of the (CCTG)n expansion in seven DM2 samples (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by QP-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The two patients with 'pure' (CCTG)n expansions based on ONT data (patients C and E) did not yield amplification peaks within the expansion range with the P4TCTG primer.
source: Interestingly, the two patients with 'pure' (CCTG)n expansions based on ONT data (patients C and E) did not yield amplification peaks within the expansion range with the P4TCTG primer (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QP-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Direct sequencing of QP-PCR products generated using primer P4TCTG confirmed the presence of (TCTG)n motif in DM2 patients A1, A2, A3, A4, B, D, and F.
source: The direct sequencing of QP-PCR products generated using primer P4TCTG confirmed the presence of (TCTG)n motif in DM2 patients A1, A2, A3, A4, B, D, and F, thus supporting the ONT data (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing of QP-PCR products shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Repeat interruptions within the expanded array have been reported in 3%–8% of DM1 patients.
source: Repeat interruptions within the expanded array have been reported in 3%–8% of DM1 patients (Tomé et al., 2018; Braida et al., 2010; Santoro et al., 2017; Santoro et al., 2013; Ballester-Lopez et al., 2020; Pešović et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2020; Radvansky et al., 2011; Siena et al., 2018; Botta et al., 2017; Santoro et al., 2015; Addis et al., 2012; Fontana et al., 2020; Lian et al., 2016; Leeflang and Arnheim, 1995; Musova et al., 2009; Cumming et al., 2018), but have not been described in DM2 before.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on DM1 repeat interruptions.

claim: Repeat interruptions have not been described in DM2 before this study.
source: Repeat interruptions within the expanded array have been reported in 3%–8% of DM1 patients (Tomé et al., 2018; Braida et al., 2010; Santoro et al., 2017; Santoro et al., 2013; Ballester-Lopez et al., 2020; Pešović et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2020; Radvansky et al., 2011; Siena et al., 2018; Botta et al., 2017; Santoro et al., 2015; Addis et al., 2012; Fontana et al., 2020; Lian et al., 2016; Leeflang and Arnheim, 1995; Musova et al., 2009; Cumming et al., 2018), but have not been described in DM2 before.
evidence: The claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the novel findings in this study.

claim: The (TCTG)n motif may have arisen through DNA duplication/repair errors or spontaneous DNA damage in the somatic cells of DM2 patients.
source: From a biological perspective, the (TCTG)n motif may have arisen through DNA duplication/repair errors or spontaneous DNA damage in the somatic cells of DM2 patients.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference about possible mechanisms.

claim: The allele length within each patient varied by 65% on average.
source: On average, the allele length within each patient varied by 65%.
evidence: The claim is supported by ONT sequencing data analysis.

claim: Extreme mosaicism has been detected when long-read sequencing is applied to other repeat-expansion disorders.
source: Extreme mosaicism (more than expected based on previous studies) has also been detected when long-read sequencing is applied to other repeat-expansion disorders, suggesting that such techniques achieve higher resolution (Loomis et al., 2013; Mizuguchi et al., 2021; Mangin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on long-read sequencing of repeat expansions.

claim: The progenitor allele length is one genetic determinant that influences the age at onset of DM2 symptoms.
source: As already demonstrated for DM1 (Cumming et al., 2019; Monckton et al., 1995), the progenitor allele length (i.e., the length of the CCTG repeat transmitted by the affected parent) is one genetic determinant that influences the age at onset of DM2 symptoms, and that age is further modified by individual-specific differences in the level of somatic instability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from DM1 studies and applied to DM2 by analogy, supported by citations.

claim: Age at onset of DM2 symptoms is further modified by individual-specific differences in the level of somatic instability.
source: As already demonstrated for DM1 (Cumming et al., 2019; Monckton et al., 1995), the progenitor allele length (i.e., the length of the CCTG repeat transmitted by the affected parent) is one genetic determinant that influences the age at onset of DM2 symptoms, and that age is further modified by individual-specific differences in the level of somatic instability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from DM1 studies and applied to DM2 by analogy, supported by citations.

claim: PCR-free analysis potentially allows the direct assessment of DNA methylation.
source: Another advantage of the approach demonstrated hereby is that PCR-free analysis potentially allows the direct assessment of DNA methylation, as already reported for other repeat-linked diseases (Fukuda et al., 2021; Giesselmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on methylation analysis using long-read sequencing.

claim: Pyrosequencing revealed hypomethylation of CpG sites upstream and hypermethylation of CpG sites downstream of the (CCTG)n expansion in DM2 patients and healthy individuals, with no significant differences between these groups.
source: The methylation of the CNBP gene has been analyzed using a pyrosequencing method, revealing hypomethylation of CpG sites upstream and hypermethylation of CpG sites downstream of the (CCTG)n expansion in DM2 patients and healthy individuals, with no significant differences between these groups (Santoro et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on CNBP methylation.

claim: The cost for Cas9-mediated sequencing of a single patient is relatively high and not comparable with the PCR-based approaches used in routine DM2 molecular diagnostics.
source: To date, the cost for Cas9-mediated sequencing of a single patient is relatively high and not comparable with the PCR-based approaches used in the routine of the DM2 molecular diagnostics.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of current costs and practical considerations.

claim: Targeted long-read sequencing might help to solve unusual large and complex (CCTG)n expansions not detectable with conventional methods.
source: Nevertheless, targeted long-read sequencing might help to solve unusual large and complex (CCTG)n expansions not detectable with conventional methods and identifies noncanonical repetitive motif conformations and sequence interruptions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the demonstrated capabilities of the method.

claim: The study achieved >500× enrichment on CNBP using the Cas9 protocol.
source: From a technical perspective, we achieved >500× enrichment on CNBP using the Cas9 protocol, which is robust and comparable to similar assays for the assessment of microsatellite length (Giesselmann et al., 2019; Mizuguchi et al., 2021; Sone et al., 2019; Wallace et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data and comparison with published literature.

claim: Multiplex enrichment protocols showed 10-fold lower enrichment with 70% unclassified reads compared to singleplex.
source: We also compared Cas9-mediated singleplex versus multiplex enrichment protocols for the first time on clinical samples and observed a consistently lower performance (10-fold lower enrichment, with 70% unclassified reads) in the multiplex environment, as reported by other ONT users for other type of samples (Oxford Nanopore Community, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data comparing singleplex and multiplex experiments.

claim: The study enrolled nine genetically confirmed DM2 Italian patients.
source: We retrospectively analyzed nine genetically confirmed DM2 Italian patients, whose enrollment in the study was approved by the institutional review board of Policlinico Tor Vergata (document no. 232/19).
evidence: The claim describes the study cohort and is stated in the methods section.

claim: Two gRNAs were designed to excise a 4.2-kbp fragment spanning the CNBP repeat on chromosome 3q21.3.
source: Accordingly, we designed two gRNAs to excise a 4.2-kbp fragment spanning the CNBP repeat on chromosome 3q21.3 (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Consensus sequences generated from the normal allele shared 99.5% identity with Sanger sequences.
source: Consensus sequences generated from the normal allele shared a high degree of identity (99.5%) and significant correlation with state-of-the-art Sanger sequences, aside from a few nucleotide positions.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ONT and Sanger sequencing data.

claim: Small discrepancies between ONT and Sanger sequences probably reflect ONT sequencing errors.
source: These inconsistences probably reflect ONT sequencing errors and could be addressed by using the most recent base-calling algorithm and eventually the more accurate Q20+ chemistry.
evidence: The claim is inferred from known limitations of ONT sequencing technology.

claim: The study demonstrated the use of Cas9-mediated enrichment and ONT long-read sequencing to analyze the full (CCTG)n expansion in DM2 patients at single-nucleotide resolution for the first time.
source: Here, we have demonstrated for the first time the use of Cas9-mediated enrichment and ONT long-read sequencing to analyze the full (CCTG)n expansion in DM2 patients at single-nucleotide resolution.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main achievement of the study.

claim: The approach simultaneously determines repeat length, structure/motif, and the extent of somatic mosaicism.
source: We were able to characterize normal and expanded CNBP alleles, simultaneously revealing the repeat length, structure/motif, and extent of somatic mosaicism, which is not possible with traditional methods, even if several are used in combination.
evidence: The claim describes the capabilities of the demonstrated approach based on the results.

claim: Traditional methods cannot simultaneously determine repeat length, structure/motif, and extent of somatic mosaicism, even when used in combination.
